title: The second strike never flew

facts.text: On 4 December 1943, Rear Admiral Charles A. Pownall's Task Force 50 struck Kwajalein and Wotje Atolls in the Marshall Islands on its way home from the Gilberts. He had six carriers, Enterprise, Essex, Lexington, Yorktown, Belleau Wood and Cowpens, with 386 aircraft.
Launching near Rongerik Atoll, the carriers sent 246 planes against Kwajalein and Wotje. They sank four cargo ships, damaged two old light cruisers and shot down 19 Japanese fighters.
One photo plane brought home a clear picture of a new bomber strip on Kwajalein Island, about 70 percent finished. It meant the Marines and soldiers would have to take both ends of the atoll at once.

The plan called for a second wave of strikes at noon, and the senior aviators in the task force pressed hard for more strikes to wipe out the Japanese aircraft that were left. Pownall chose caution, and the second strike was never flown.
Japanese torpedo planes came after the carriers as they withdrew. At 2333 that night a torpedo hit Lexington in the stern, killing nine men, wounding 35 and knocking out her steering.
Lexington settled five feet by the stern and circled to port through the smoke. Her crew sealed off the flooded compartments and rigged a hand operated emergency steering gear.
She made Pearl Harbor on 9 December and went on to Bremerton, Washington, for two months of shipyard repairs.
Beside Pownall's recommendations in his report on the raid, someone wrote in pencil, in recognizable handwriting, "all defensive."

Vice Admiral John H. Towers, the Pacific Fleet's air commander, pushed to have Pownall relieved. Towers wrote that he was "overcautious in plans and operations" and that his "lack of aggressiveness" was "resented by subordinates."

The payoff came within two months. When the fast carriers sailed in January 1944 to cover the invasion of Kwajalein, they were Task Force 58 under Rear Admiral Marc A. Mitscher. Pownall took over Towers's old shore job as air commander of the Pacific Fleet and never led a combat command again.

photoNote: Tier: green. A Japanese torpedo bomber blowing apart in midair after a direct hit by a 5 inch shell from an American carrier during an attack off Kwajalein; flaming wreckage streams across the water, a column of smoke at right, a ship's antenna mast in the left foreground. U.S. Navy photo, National Archives 80-G-415001 (naId 520751), use Unrestricted, NARA dates it December 1943. Pacific Wrecks credits it to Photographer's Mate A. N. Cooperman aboard USS Yorktown, 4 December 1943, and it ran full page in Life. Cropped from the scanned print mount (NARA TIFF 2465 x 3000) to 1554 x 1920, portrait. Chosen for drama: the counterattack that came after Pownall pulled back, caught at the instant of the hit. Pacific Wrecks calls the plane a Jill, other captions a Kate, so the caption should just say torpedo bomber. Runner up: Lexington from USS Cowpens during the Marshalls raids, November to December 1943, color, 80-G-K-102.
photoCredit: A Japanese torpedo bomber explodes after a hit by a carrier's 5 inch gun off Kwajalein, December 1943. U.S. Navy photo, National Archives 80-G-415001, public domain.

videoPhotos.credit: USS Lexington seen from USS Cowpens during the Marshalls and Gilberts raids, November to December 1943. U.S. Navy color photo 80-G-K-102, National Archives, public domain.
USS Lexington underway during the Gilberts operation, seen from USS Monterey, late 1943. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-366924, National Archives, public domain.
Lt. Cmdr. Paul D. Buie briefs VF-16 pilots aboard Lexington, November to December 1943. Photo by Cmdr. Edward Steichen, U.S. Navy color photo 80-G-K-16053, public domain.
A VF-16 Hellcat gets the takeoff flag aboard Lexington, 23 November 1943. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-44605, National Archives, public domain.

declassified.fact: Not all the damage that day came from the Japanese. During the counterattacks the light cruiser Mobile was hurt when one of her own 5 inch mounts accidentally fired into one of her 40 millimeter mounts, and the destroyer Taylor was hit by friendly fire from the cruiser Oakland.

film.license: U.S. Navy film, public domain (NARA use status Undetermined, its usual note for 428-NPC)
film.shot_notes: Whole reel, 6 min 23 s, faded color, silent. NOON (this card): 00:14 to 00:36 antiaircraft bursts and a plane attacking ships at sea (open at 00:16 on the bursts); 00:52 to 01:12 aerials of an atoll's reef; 02:36 to 02:52 smoke rising from the atoll. The Hellcat crash and fire (01:16 to 02:10) and the TBF and F6F formations (05:28 to 06:00) belong to No. 118's 7 p.m. video. 03:20 to 03:56 men in pith helmets under palms (unidentified, avoid).
film.date_note: NARA dates the reel 19 Dec 1943 and titles it the air attacks on the Marshall and Gilbert Islands, which covers the November and December 1943 carrier strikes; it is not dated to 4 Dec. Caption as Navy film of the carrier raids on the Gilberts and Marshalls, late 1943.

video.note: 428-NPC-1007 (NARA 75781), faded color Navy film, silent. Cut 27 Nov 2026 inside research's noon stretches: 00:16.7 to 00:23.85 splashes and antiaircraft fire among ships at sea, a plane attacking (opening); 00:25.7 to 00:29.35 antiaircraft bursts and a plane going down in flames; 00:59.6 to 01:03.45 aerial of an atoll's reef. Cropped to drop the burned in timecode along the bottom and the black film edges; 10:11 pixels scaled to square. Nothing from No. 118's stretches (01:16 to 02:10, 05:28 to 06:00).
